en: The Philippine Eagle, our national bird, has distinct brown and white feathers and a shaggy crest observable in the forests of Mindanao.
The sampaguita, our national flower, is a white jasmine with a strong sweet scent that blooms on climbing vines in local gardens.
The narra, our national tree, produces hard red wood and small yellow flowers that you can see in many Philippine parks.
The Ifugao people carved the Banaue Rice Terraces into the mountains, creating observable stepped fields that follow the natural contours of the land.
During the Pahiyas Festival in Lucban, locals decorate their houses with colorful kiping, which are leaf-shaped wafers made from ground rice.
National Scientist Angel Alcala studied Philippine coral reefs, observing how diverse marine life thrives in the colorful underwater ecosystems he helped protect.
During his exile in Dapitan, hero Jose Rizal planted hundreds of tropical trees and built a water system using local gravity and springs.
The bangus, or milkfish, is our national fish, recognizable by its smooth silver scales and streamlined body as it swims in coastal waters.
The T'boli women of Mindanao weave T'nalak cloth from the fibers of the abaca plant, which grows abundantly in volcanic soil.
The Department of Environment and Natural Resources protects the rare Rafflesia, a giant red flower observable blooming on the forest floor.
The Philippine pearl, our national gem, forms as a smooth, lustrous sphere inside the shell of the local pearl oyster.
National Scientist Gavino Trono studied local seaweeds, observing how different species of red and green algae grow in our tidal zones.
